headline: US proposes up to 25 percent tariff on India as markets extend rally

segments.title: The big picture
segments.script:
Good morning. It's Thursday, the twenty-sixth of November, and here is your Market Brief.

Three things matter most today. First, Washington has put a number on the table. The US Trade Representative has proposed tariffs of up to 25 percent on Indian goods, dropping to 17 percent if India signs a trade deal. Second, the market has shrugged it off so far. After their best session since the sixth of November, the Sensex and Nifty are higher again this morning, led by IT stocks and steady foreign buying. And third, inflation worries are building at home. Consumer inflation rose to 6.1 percent in October, and more voices now expect the Reserve Bank to raise rates in December.

segments.title: How markets closed
segments.script:
Wednesday was a strong day. The Sensex rose 1.82 percent and the Nifty 1.85 percent, wiping out Monday's losses. Falling oil and a firmer rupee lifted banks and consumer stocks. Bank Nifty gained over 2 percent, and Hindustan Unilever had its best day since June 2024. Nestle India, Tata Consumer, InterGlobe Aviation and HDFC Life were among the top gainers. Metals lagged, with Tata Steel, Hindalco and JSW Steel down, along with Shriram Finance and Max Healthcare.

The flows were the real story. Foreign institutional investors bought about 4,479 crore rupees of shares. Domestic institutions bought about 4,019 crore rupees, only their second day of net buying this month.

This morning, the rally has carried on. Around twenty past eleven, the Sensex was up about 444 points at 84,383, and the Nifty near 25,917, after touching 25,950 earlier. Nifty IT jumped over 2 percent, with Wipro up 4 percent on a partnership with bp, and Infosys and HCL Tech also strong. Mid caps and small caps are up too. HDFC Bank has climbed 30 percent from its October low and has overtaken Bharti Airtel to become the second most valuable listed company. Sugar stocks like Balrampur Chini, Dhampur and Shree Renuka jumped as much as 14 percent after the industry body forecast a decade-low sugar crop. It is also the Sensex monthly expiry today.

For levels, analysts at Moneycontrol see 26,000 as the hurdle, with support around 25,500 to 25,600. Analyst Jatin Gedia thinks the Nifty could head for its all-time high of 26,373 and possibly 26,600.

segments.title: IPOs and deals
segments.script:
Crystal Crop Protection made a modest debut today. After being subscribed 17 times, it listed at 278 rupees on the NSE, about 2 percent above its issue price of 272, and at 280 on the BSE. Foodlink F and B Holdings, a 361 crore rupee issue, opened yesterday. It was 23 percent subscribed on day one, with the retail portion fully booked. Brokerages are split: Anand Rathi says subscribe for the long term, while SBI Securities is neutral. Allotment is expected on the first of December and listing on the third.

Now to the big block deals. LG Electronics of South Korea is selling up to 2 percent of its Indian arm, worth about 2,320 crore rupees, to meet minimum public shareholding rules by the end of December. The stock fell 3 percent. Carlyle sold a 7.4 percent stake in Piramal Pharma for over 2,211 crore rupees, cutting its holding to about 10.5 percent, with Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund the largest buyer.

In deal financing, Deutsche Bank and Punjab National Bank have signed a pact to fund acquisitions, after rules now let Indian lenders fund up to 75 percent of a deal. State Bank of India has a similar tie-up with Mitsubishi UFJ. And the Cabinet has cleared Prudential's foreign investment in Bharti Life Insurance.

Exchanges are in the spotlight too. The NSE is now the world's third-largest stock exchange by market value, ahead of Deutsche Boerse and the London Stock Exchange. BSE shares hit a four-month high after HDFC Securities upgraded them, and HSBC started coverage with a positive view.

One more boardroom battle to note. Tata Trusts has decided to go to the Bombay High Court against N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons chairman. Reports say Shapoor Mistry has written to the Prime Minister twice pushing for a Tata Sons listing. The Tata Sons board meets on the thirtieth.

segments.title: Results roundup
segments.script:
A quiet day for results, with one standout. Siemens Energy India posted an 81.5 percent jump in net profit to 653 crore rupees for the September quarter, helped by more exports and steady order execution. It declared a dividend of 12 rupees a share, and the stock rose 9 percent.

In orders, Jupiter Wagons is up about 30 percent in two days after forming a joint venture with South Korea's Woojin Industrial Systems to make metro coaches in India. And Jyoti Structures rose 9 percent on a 272 crore rupee transmission line order from Sterlite Power.

segments.title: Economy and policy
segments.script:
Let's start with prices. Consumer inflation rose to 6.1 percent in October from 5.5 percent in September. A Reserve Bank paper says price rises are now spreading across more categories. Its monthly bulletin still calls the economy resilient, with strong credit demand and exports, and says the pass-through of the oil shock has been limited.

On rates, S and P Global now expects the Reserve Bank to raise rates in December and again in early 2027. It has cut its growth forecast for next year to 7 percent. The chief investment officer at Baroda BNP Paribas Mutual Fund also expects a quarter-point hike in December.

On the external side, the numbers are mixed. Net foreign direct investment turned negative in September, at minus 4.95 billion dollars, as inflows slowed and repatriation rose. The Reserve Bank bought a net 6.94 billion dollars that month, its fourth straight month of buying, and its forward dollar short book hit a record of about 239 billion dollars. It has also moved 60 tonnes of gold home in six months, so 84 percent of its gold is now held in India. And it is checking whether importers are splitting forex deals below 2 million dollars to dodge extra reserve rules.

In policy, the Cabinet approved an 11,000 crore rupee scheme for construction equipment, with sales-linked incentives of 8 to 13 percent over five years. The Finance Minister held her twelfth pre-Budget meeting, and the government may assume crude at 80 to 85 dollars for next year's Budget. One worry: the sugar crop is seen at a decade low of 26.52 million tonnes after weak rains.

segments.title: Around the world
segments.script:
The tariff news first. The United States has proposed new duties on fourteen trading partners over what it calls excess industrial capacity, with China facing the steepest. India's proposed rate is the second highest, at up to 25 percent, or 17 percent with a deal. Washington also took aim at Make in India and the production-linked incentive schemes. India has rejected the charge. Jefferies notes that a large part of India's 104 billion dollars of exports to the US falls outside this framework, and the Global Trade Research Initiative says 17 percent would give India a small edge over Asian rivals. Indian traders, though, want a 25 percent retaliatory duty if the higher rate goes ahead.

On oil, Brent is back in the low nineties, after the Houthis claimed a strike on a Saudi refinery and tankers were reported hit by mines near Hormuz.

On Wall Street, it was a wild session ahead of today's Thanksgiving holiday. The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 percent from its October peak, bear market territory, before recovering much of the loss. Nvidia still ended down 3.9 percent. Asian markets are higher this morning as buyers step back into the AI trade.

segments.title: Stories you're following
segments.script: An update on the India and US trade deal you're following. Just a week after India said signing must wait for Washington's new tariff rules, those rules have arrived in draft: 17 percent with a deal, up to 25 percent without. That gives both sides a clear reason to close the deal soon.

segments.title: Your money
segments.script:
Some useful changes for your money. From the twenty-fourth of December, the Securities and Exchange Board of India is simplifying KYC. Your extra KYC details will sit with the KYC registration agencies, so you won't have to submit them again for every new demat or mutual fund account. The regulator has also warned investors not to rely on grey market premiums when applying for IPOs.

For salaried readers, the provident fund body plans to allow PF withdrawals through UPI by the end of December, with a minimum of 1,000 rupees. Central government dearness allowance has gone up 3 points to 63 percent of basic pay, and several states have followed. Pensioners, remember the thirtieth of November deadline for your life certificate.

A tax ruling worth knowing. The Delhi bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal deleted an addition of 12.09 lakh rupees for a taxpayer who showed that cash deposited in his account was repayment of a loan he had given. The borrower denied the loan, but its own balance sheets backed his claim.

On gold, it has been a bumpy ride. It touched a one-year low on fears of more US rate hikes, then bounced back on MCX this morning, with silver rising faster. Gold loans, meanwhile, have grown 61 percent in a year to 23.3 lakh crore rupees. And credit card spending rose 20 percent in October to 2.45 lakh crore rupees, on festive shopping.

That's your Market Brief. Today, watch whether the Nifty can get past 26,000 on expiry day, how the government formally answers the US tariff proposal, and whether foreign investors keep buying. Oil near the low nineties is the other thing to keep an eye on. Have a good day.
